title: Q4 Planning — Routing v3 & Driver App

chapters.title: Kickoff and agenda
chapters.gist: Asher frames the goal: leave with Q4 priorities the team believes in, given roughly 11 engineers of capacity, and lays out the agenda.

chapters.title: Q3 in review
chapters.gist: Routing v3 beta beat its targets (11% fewer miles, on-time 91.2% to 94.6%), Ravi recaps the Sep 24 outage and late status page, Sofia relays Brightside's frustration, and Tom says pipeline is strong with Harbor & Pine as the big deal.

chapters.title: Routing v3 GA scope
chapters.gist: Daniel walks through what ships in Routing v3 GA on Nov 17, Kenji explains that the ETA model is much weaker on dense urban and loading-dock stops, and the group decides urban-dense mode ships behind a per-fleet flag, off by default.

chapters.title: The live ETA collision
chapters.gist: Tom admits he told Harbor & Pine live ETA sharing would be ready this quarter, Maya pushes back that it's about 5 engineer-weeks nobody has planned, Sofia ties it to Brightside's renewal and Sacramento expansion, Priya points out it's a design project too, and Asher slows the discussion down before a decision.

chapters.title: Driver app onboarding
chapters.gist: Priya shows that 38% of new drivers drop off before their first route and proposes a new flow (phone login, permissions primer, practice route) to get below 15%; it needs about two frontend engineers, which depends on hiring Sam Rivera and possibly a contractor.

chapters.title: Reliability follow-ups
chapters.gist: Ravi asks for one engineer for three weeks to add retry budgets with jitter, a circuit breaker on the ETA service, and an automated status page; Daniel calls it non-negotiable and the group agrees it goes first.

chapters.title: The trade-off and the decision
chapters.gist: Asher proposes Live ETA v0 (a tracking link with ETA and status timeline, no live map, about 2.5 engineer-weeks, shipping Nov 6), with the full map in Q1, onboarding starting Nov 2 with a contractor, and reliability first; Maya agrees if Tom resets Harbor & Pine in writing, and Kenji's idea to show an ETA range instead of a point time is adopted.

chapters.title: Q4 OKRs, owners and wrap-up
chapters.gist: Asher restates the four Q4 OKRs with owners and key dates, Priya and Tom adjust their key results, Ravi's reliability targets become a health metric, and the meeting closes with next steps due Oct 5 to Oct 23.

turns.t: Okay, I think — is that everyone? I see Maya, Daniel, Priya. Kenji, hi. Ravi. Sofia's here. Tom's — Tom said he's two minutes out, he's coming off a call with Harbor & Pine, so let's just start and he can catch up.
Hi. Hello.
Works for me.
Can you hear me okay? I switched headsets, this one's been kind of flaky.
You're good. A little quiet, but good.
Okay. Better?

Better. So, okay. Thanks everyone for doing this on a Friday afternoon, I know for some of you it's the last meeting of the week and you'd rather be anywhere else. The goal today is simple to say and hard to do. We have to leave this call with Q4 priorities that we actually believe in. Not a wish list. And the constraint is capacity. Maya and I went through it on Wednesday and it's about eleven engineers, call it eleven, for the quarter, and that's before holidays and on-call eat into it.

Eleven-ish. Eleven is generous, honestly. Once you take out on-call, Thanksgiving week, and the December freeze starting the 14th, it's more like nine and a half engineers of actual building time. And most of that is already spoken for by v3 GA. I'll get into the math when we hit the trade-offs, but I want everyone walking in knowing it's tight.

Which is exactly why we're doing this as one meeting and not five separate ones. So, the agenda. First, ten minutes or less on Q3, where we landed. Then Routing v3 GA scope, because that's the thing we've committed to and the date's not moving. Then the — the stuff that's competing for whatever's left. Live ETA sharing, driver onboarding, and Ravi's reliability follow-ups from the outage. Then we make the call, and then OKRs and owners. I'd like us to actually decide things today. If we walk out with 'let's take it offline' on everything, I've failed.
Hey, sorry, sorry — I'm here. What did I miss?
Nothing yet. You're right on time for the part where I say we're deciding things today.
Great. Love that. Love deciding things.
He says that now.
I say it every time, Sofia.

Okay, one ground rule. The docs are all in the folder — the capacity sheet, the beta report, Priya's onboarding funnel. I'm not going to screen-share all of them. If you need a number, ask, and whoever owns it answers. Cool? Okay. Maya, do you want to do the Q3 numbers or should I?
You start, I'll jump in.

So, Q3. The headline is Routing v3 beta. We've had six fleets on it since September 8th, and the results are honestly better than I expected. Eleven percent fewer miles driven — that's across all six, weighted — and on-time delivery went from 91.2 to 94.6 percent. Which, for context, the target we set back in the spring was 93.
That's the slide. That's the slide I want in every deck.

And it's held up, which is the part I care about. It's not like week one was great and then it decayed. Week four was actually the best week. On the engineering side, quick scorecard. We shipped the solver migration, the beta rollout tooling, and the new dispatch board filters. What slipped was the CSV import rewrite, about three weeks, mostly because we pulled two people onto beta support when the second beta fleet had that whole depot geocoding mess. I'd make that trade again. But it's why I'm allergic to anything unplanned this quarter. Every time we've said it's just a couple of weeks this year, it's been double.
It has been double. I have the receipts.
He does have the receipts.

One caveat, small one. The eleven percent is miles, not time. Drive-time savings are more like eight, eight and a half, because the solver is happy to take a slightly slower road if it saves distance. Nobody's complained. But if sales says 'eleven percent faster,' that's wrong.
Noted. Fewer miles, not faster. Got it.
And part of the on-time number is the ETA model. Mean absolute error went from 6.1 to 4.3 minutes on the beta fleets. I'll talk about where it's still bad later.

Yeah, let's save that for GA scope. And good catch, Daniel, on miles versus time. Okay, and then the not-great part of Q3. Ravi, can you do the short version of the 24th? Short version — we did the long version in the retro.

Yeah. So Thursday, September 24th, the ETA service was down for forty-seven minutes, 14:12 to 14:59 UTC. Root cause: the Redis cluster did a failover, which on its own should've been a blip, but the dispatch workers all retried at once — no backoff, no jitter — and that retry storm knocked the ETA service over. Three hundred and twelve fleets affected. Drivers saw stale ETAs and end customers got wrong delivery windows. And — I'll just say it — the status page was updated twenty-six minutes in. That's on us. That's on me, really.
It's on the process, not just you.
Sure, but right now I'm the process. Anyway. I've got follow-ups, I'll get to them in the reliability section.

Can I add the customer side for a second? Because Brightside was the loudest one. Jordan called me directly, which he doesn't do. Their drivers were staring at ETAs that were forty minutes old, and their customers got texts saying 'arriving 2:15' for orders that showed up at three-something. Groceries. Ice cream melting, the whole thing. And Aisha, their fleet manager, told me her dispatch team was refreshing our status page and it said 'all systems operational' for almost half an hour. That's the part that stung.
Yeah. Yeah, that's fair.

And — this matters for later — Jordan, on that same call, brought up live ETA sharing again. That's the second time he's asked. He said, more or less, 'if my customers could see where the van actually is, the outage would've been half as bad.' I don't know if that's true, but that's how he feels.
Okay, let's hold that, because that's like forty percent of today.
Holding it. Just flagging, renewal is January 31st and they're at a hundred and forty-five K.
Can I do pipeline real quick?
Go.

So, pipeline is strong. Genuinely — not sales-strong, actually strong. The big one, obviously, is Harbor & Pine. Four hundred and twenty trucks, regional freight in the Pacific Northwest. About three-ten ARR, which would be our biggest logo by a lot. Decision is October 30th. We're up against RouteWise, who are cheaper — I'll be honest, they're cheaper by a meaningful amount. Marcus Hill, their ops director, is our champion and he's great, he gets it. But the CFO, Dana Whitfield, is the one signing, and we've never been on a call with her.
Never?
Never. Marcus says she reads the summary and decides. So whatever Marcus brings her is what we've got.
And integrations? Last I heard, Elena had questions about the TMS.

Elena's fine. Well — Elena's fine-ish. They run Samsara for telematics, which is easy, we've done that a dozen times. And an old on-prem Oracle TMS, which is less easy. But she's not a blocker, she's just thorough.
Thorough is fine. Oracle on-prem is the part that eats a week.
Sure. Anyway — beyond Harbor & Pine we've got three mid-size grocery deals in late stage, and all three want v3. So GA landing on time matters for them too, not just for the OKR.
Which three?

The two regional grocery chains in Texas, and the parcel fleet in Denver that did the pilot over the summer. Together they're about the same ARR as Harbor & Pine, give or take, but they're three separate signatures, so the risk is spread out. All three asked about v3 timing in the last two weeks. One of them asked about live tracking too, but casually. Not a must-have.

Okay. Good to know it's not just one deal holding up the quarter. Okay. So Q3 in one sentence: v3 works, the outage hurt us with exactly the customer we can't afford to hurt, and the pipeline is real but the biggest deal depends on someone we've never met.
That's bleak. But accurate.

Can I sneak one thing in? On the driver app side, Q3 was mostly research. We did the funnel analysis and nineteen interviews with new drivers. I'll show the numbers in the onboarding section, but the short version is the drop-off is worse than we thought it was.
How much worse?
I'll save it. It's a good reveal.
She's building suspense.
I'm building a narrative, Tom.
Fine, fine. Okay. Moving on.
Okay, v3 GA. Daniel, you've got the scope doc. Walk us through it, and flag anything that's at risk.

Sure. So, GA is November 17th, that hasn't changed. What's in: the new solver becomes the default for every new fleet starting that day. Existing fleets get a migration wizard — they can opt in at GA, and we want everyone moved by end of January. Kenji's ETA model replaces the old heuristic ETAs for anyone on v3. Time windows and driver break rules, which the beta fleets have been using. And API parity with v2, which is the boring part that takes the longest, honestly, because there are like four endpoints that nobody documented and three customers depend on.
Two customers. We killed one of those dependencies last week.

Two. Even better. What's out of GA: multi-day routes and EV charging constraints. Both go to Q1, and I've already told the two beta fleets who asked about EV, so nobody's surprised. Code freeze for GA is November 10th. The rollout is staged — twenty-five percent of eligible fleets on the 17th, then fifty the week after, and everyone eligible by December 1st, before the holiday freeze. The migration wizard is the piece I'd watch. It's a lot of edge cases. Depots with weird geocodes, fleets with custom service times, that kind of thing.

And for staffing, GA is taking six of the eleven through November. Daniel's leading it, three on solver and API parity, Kenji on the model, and one floating between the migration wizard and beta support. I'm not moving anyone off that until we're past December 1st. That's the one thing I'm going to be stubborn about today.
That's fair. GA is the one we've told the board about.
And the beta fleets just — they stay on, right? They don't get flipped back or anything?
They stay on. They're basically already GA, they just don't know it.
Love that. Can I put 'eleven percent fewer miles' on the website yet? Leah's been asking me for a case study from one of the beta fleets, and I keep telling her to wait.
Talk to Leah offline. Use one fleet that's agreed to be named, and use Daniel's wording — miles, not time.
And please not the fleet with the depot geocoding problem. Their first two weeks were a mess.
Ha. Yeah. Noted.
What's at risk?
Two things. API parity, which I just said, and that's a known amount of grind, I'm not worried about it. The real one is the ETA model in certain conditions. Kenji should explain it, it's his.

Okay. So the 4.3 minute number is real, but it's an average across everything. When I break it down by stop type, it's very uneven. Suburban residential, it's under four minutes, it's good. Dense urban stops — downtown, apartment buildings, places where parking takes longer than the drive — the error is about 8.9 minutes. And loading docks are worse. If there's a dock wait, the error is around twelve minutes, and the tail is long. Some stops are off by thirty.
Thirty minutes?

On some stops. Not many. The problem is we don't observe the dock wait. The driver arrives, the truck sits, and we only see that it left later. So the model has nothing to learn from. For urban, I built a mode that uses dwell-time priors by building type and time of day. It helps. In the two beta fleets that are mostly urban, it brings the error down to around six. But it's only tested on those two fleets.
So the question is whether urban-dense mode is in GA or not.
Yes.
Can I — sorry, just to be the sales guy for a second. Harbor & Pine is basically all loading docks. Regional freight. Every stop is a dock.
Yes. That's the twelve-minute number.
Okay. That's — okay. Good to know before Marcus finds out on his own.

Which, to be clear, we tell them. If Marcus asks how accurate our ETAs are, the honest answer is 4.3 minutes on average, and docks are the hardest case, and that's exactly where their data would help. That's a better answer than pretending.
No, I agree. I'd rather it come from us. Elena's going to look at the numbers anyway, she's that kind of person.

And for Brightside it's the urban one. Two of their three metros are pretty dense. If we turn on v3 for them and the ETAs are off by nine minutes on half their stops, we're going to hear about it. After the outage, they're not going to give us the benefit of the doubt.

Which is why I don't want urban-dense on by default. Six minutes on two fleets is promising, it's not validated. If we make it the default for everyone and it does something weird on a fleet with a different mix, that's a GA regression on the headline feature.
But if it's better for urban fleets, why wouldn't we — I mean, why ship the worse thing to Brightside on purpose?
Because we don't know it's better for Brightside. We know it's better for two fleets that aren't Brightside.
Fair. Okay. Fair.
So the options are, one, hold it out of GA entirely; two, ship it behind a flag, off by default, we turn it on per fleet; three, on by default. Nobody's arguing for three. Is anyone arguing for one?
Not me. A flag's cheap. The code's already there.
Mine too, as long as the flag has an end date. I don't want this to become one of those flags that lives in the codebase for three years and nobody remembers what it does.
We decide on the default by end of January. On or delete. That's the deal.
And I want per-fleet monitoring on it. An ETA error dashboard split by mode before we turn it on for anyone new. Otherwise we're flying blind.
I can build that dashboard. I mostly have it already, it's a notebook. I'd just need to make it a real one.
And can we turn it on for Brightside? Like, as the first one?

I'd want a week of shadow mode first. Run it next to the normal model, don't show it to anyone, compare. If it's better, then yes. Shadow mode is easy for me. The model runs on every route anyway. I'd log both predictions and compare them against the actual arrival times. After a week, we'd have enough stops in their two dense metros to know.
A week is fine. I can tell Jordan we're tuning ETAs for dense metros specifically for them. He'll like that, honestly. It sounds like attention.

Small thing — if it's behind a flag, does the dispatcher see which mode a route is using? Because if a dispatcher's comparing two routes and one's on urban-dense and the ETAs look different, they're going to file a bug.
Good point. Probably a little badge in the route detail. Not a big UI thing.
I can give you a badge. Badges I can do.

Okay, so let me say it back. Urban-dense mode ships in GA behind a per-fleet flag, off by default. Kenji turns the notebook into a real ETA error dashboard split by mode. Brightside goes into a week of shadow mode, and if it's better, they're the first fleet we flip. And the loading-dock problem is open — we don't have a fix for it this quarter. Is that right?
Yes. For docks, I'd need dock-wait data. Harbor & Pine's Samsara data might actually have it, if they ever sign.
There's a sentence I'm putting in the proposal. 'Your data makes us better.'
Please run that sentence past Kenji before it goes anywhere.
Obviously.
Okay. Decided. GA scope otherwise stays as Daniel described it. Anything else on GA before we go to the hard part?
Just that the ETA service is the thing that fell over on the 24th, and GA puts more traffic on it. So I'd like the reliability work done before the rollout ramps. I'll make the case later.
Noted. Okay. The hard part.

So, live ETA sharing. The customer-facing tracking link. Driver location on a map, ETA, the whole thing. It's not built, it's not in anyone's plan, and two of our most important accounts want it. Tom, you said you wanted to say something before we started this one.

Yeah. So, I'd rather you hear it from me now than from Marcus later. On the call with Harbor & Pine on Tuesday — Marcus, Elena, two of their dispatch leads — we were going through their must-haves list, and we were doing great, honestly. Samsara, fine. Time windows, fine. Then Marcus asked about a tracking link for their shippers. Their shippers call dispatch all day asking where the truck is, and it's a big part of why they're looking at new software at all. And I told him it would be ready this quarter.
You told him what?
That it'd be ready this quarter. I didn't give a date. I didn't say GA. But I said 'this quarter,' and he wrote it down. And I think it's in the evaluation doc he's putting together for Dana.
So it's in writing. In front of the CFO.
Probably. Yes. I haven't seen the doc.

Tom. It's about five engineer-weeks. Nobody has it in plan. It's not on the capacity sheet, it's not in a design doc, we haven't even agreed what it is. You can't — I'm sorry, but you can't commit engineering time on a sales call. We had this exact conversation in June, with the bulk import thing for that parcel fleet, and we ended up pulling two people off v3 for three weeks to cover it. Three weeks. That's part of why the CSV rewrite slipped. So I'm not being precious about process, I'm telling you what it actually costs.

I know. I know we did. And I'm not saying it was right. But I want you to understand the situation I was in. RouteWise has a tracking link. It's ugly, but it exists. Marcus asked me, point blank, 'can you match it,' and if I say 'maybe Q1,' that's three-ten in ARR walking to the cheaper vendor who already has the feature.

And if you say 'this quarter' and we deliver in February, we've lost the trust of our biggest customer before they've even onboarded. That's worse. That's way worse. I'd rather lose the deal honestly than win it on something we can't ship.
That's easy to say when it's not your number.
It's my team's weekends, Tom. That's my number.
Can I just — can I finish the —
Sorry. Go.
I'm not saying it was right. I'm saying the alternative wasn't free either. If I'd said Q1, I'm pretty sure we'd be second choice right now, and second choice against the cheaper vendor is losing.
Okay —
Can I — sorry —
Go ahead.
No, you go, Daniel.
No, really, go.

Okay. Just — I want to make sure this doesn't turn into a Harbor & Pine-only conversation. Brightside has asked for this twice. Jordan asked in August, and again after the outage. It's tied to the renewal, which is January 31st, and it's tied to Sacramento. They want to add a fourth metro, sixty more vans, and Jordan said pretty directly that he doesn't want to roll out a new metro without a tracking link for their customers. So this isn't just Tom's deal. This is retention plus expansion on a customer we already have.
Mm-hm. Yeah.

And timing-wise, Jordan wants to launch Sacramento in March. So he's deciding on the expansion around the same time as the renewal. If we show up in January with nothing, I think we keep the renewal, probably, but the sixty vans go to whoever has a tracking link. I don't want to oversell it, but that's my read.
I'm not saying nobody wants it. I'm saying everybody wants it and nobody's paying for it in capacity.
That's fair. I'm just adding weight to the 'wants it' side.

Okay, my thing was technical. The five weeks is for the full version. Driver app streams location every few seconds, we need a tokenized public link with expiry, a little web page with a live map, map tiles, which cost money at scale, and the whole thing has to degrade gracefully. And I'd point out the last time the ETA service had a bad day, every one of those links would've been showing garbage to end customers. Which is a lot more public than a dispatcher's screen.
Can I ask one thing? Which ETA would the link show?
Yours. The model's. Same one dispatchers see.
Okay. That's — okay. I'll think about that.
Yeah, that's — I'd want that thing behind the circuit breaker I'm about to ask for. Just saying.
Say more?

Sure. Right now, if Redis fails over, the ETA service doesn't fail cleanly, it fails slowly and keeps serving old data. That's annoying on a dispatcher screen. On a public link, with a customer's name on it, it's a support ticket per stop. So whatever we build here, it can't go out before the reliability fixes.

And can I add — it's not just an engineering project. It's a design project. This is the first time we put something in front of the end customer. Not the fleet, not the dispatcher. The person waiting for their groceries or their pallet. What does it look like on a phone? Is it branded as Brightside or as Tandem? Do we show the driver's exact location — like, the driver's location while they're at another customer's house? There are privacy questions. What do we show when the ETA is stale, which, again, the 24th. None of that is designed. I haven't had a single hour on it. If I'm honest, the full map version is two weeks of design minimum before an engineer should touch it, and that's if we don't do a round of testing with real end customers, which we should.
Okay. That's — yeah. I hadn't thought about the driver privacy piece at all.
Drivers will think about it. Trust me. In the interviews, two of them brought up being tracked without me asking.
So it's five engineer-weeks plus design time we haven't counted, plus reliability work it depends on. And Tom told the biggest prospect we've ever had it's coming this quarter.
Yes. I said that. I'm owning it. I'm not trying to wriggle out. I'm trying to figure out what we do now.

Okay. Let's slow down for a second, because I think everyone's right about something, and if we keep going like this we'll just get louder. Tom, I appreciate you saying it up front. Seriously. It would've been a lot worse to find out from Marcus in three weeks. Maya, you're right that we can't run the roadmap through sales calls, and I'll take the process part of that with Tom separately, it's not a this-meeting thing.
Yeah. That's fair. I'll take that.
Okay. Thank you.

What I want to do now is separate two questions. One, what does Harbor & Pine actually need, as opposed to what was asked for. And two, what can we actually build. Tom, what's the actual problem on Marcus's side? Not the feature. The problem.

The problem is phone calls. Their shippers and receivers call dispatch constantly asking 'where's my truck, when's it showing up.' Marcus told me dispatch spends something like a third of their day on those calls. Dana sees that as headcount. That's the thing she cares about.
So the problem is 'when will it arrive,' not 'show me a dot moving on a map.'

I mean, the dot is nice. The dot's in the RouteWise demo. But yeah — the calls are the 'when.' And to be fair to Marcus, he's not a feature-list guy. He's an ops guy. He told me the RouteWise demo was slick but their ETAs were off half the time when they piloted it. So he doesn't actually trust the dot. He just knows Dana's going to see it in the side-by-side.
Same for Brightside, honestly. Jordan's complaint is customers not knowing when the van's coming. Nobody's ever said the word 'map' to me. They said 'tracking link.'

Okay. Hold that thought, because I think there's a smaller version of this. But I don't want to design it in the room before we've looked at onboarding and reliability, because those are drawing from the same pool. Maya, can you put the actual numbers up? What's free after GA?

Sure. After v3 GA, the integrations work we've already committed to, on-call, Thanksgiving, and the freeze, we have roughly nine engineer-weeks unallocated before December 14th. Nine. Full live ETA is five, plus whatever design adds. Ravi's about to ask for three. Priya needs two frontend engineers for onboarding, which is way more than what's left. So — you can see the problem. We can do maybe two of the three, and only if one of them gets smaller.
Or we hire.
We are hiring. Nobody we hire in October is shipping production code in November.
Okay, what about pulling one person off GA for two weeks? Just two. GA's in good shape, Daniel said so himself.

No. Sorry, but no. GA is in good shape because nobody's been pulled off it. It's the one date we've told the board, and the migration wizard is exactly the kind of thing that looks done until a real fleet hits it. I said at the start I'd be stubborn about one thing. That's the thing.
I'm with Maya on that one. If you pull someone in October, you pay for it in the week of the 17th.
Okay. Okay. Had to ask.
Okay. Let's do onboarding next and come back to this with all three on the table.
Okay, Priya. Your big reveal.

Okay. So. Thirty-eight percent. Thirty-eight percent of new drivers who install the driver app never complete their first route. They download it, they get stuck somewhere, and either they call their dispatcher or they just quit. We thought it was somewhere around twenty, based on the support tickets, but the tickets only catch the people who complain. The funnel catches everyone.
Thirty-eight. Wow.
Is that drivers quitting the job, or quitting the app?

Good question, and it's mostly the app. Some of them quit the job, sure, delivery has high churn anyway. But when we called people, most of them were still driving. They were just using paper or texting the dispatcher. Which means the fleet is paying for a seat that's not being used, and their routes aren't optimized, and their ETAs are — honestly, made up.
That matches what I hear. Aisha at Brightside told me she has one dispatcher who basically spends Monday mornings onboarding new drivers by hand. Sitting next to them, tapping through the screens.

Yeah, that's the pattern. So, where do they drop? Three places. First is login. Right now it's email and password. A lot of drivers don't have an email they check, or they share a phone, or they set a password on day one and forget it by day three. That's about a third of the drop. Second is permissions. We ask for location 'always' and notifications back to back, with the system dialogs and zero context. People say no, because why would you say yes to 'always' from an app you've never used, and then the app basically doesn't work and gives them no clue why. That's the biggest single step. And third is the first route itself. It's live. Real stops, real customers, dispatcher watching. Several drivers said some version of 'I didn't want to mess it up so I just didn't start.'
That last one is kind of heartbreaking.
It is. One guy told me he drove the whole route with the app closed because he was scared tapping 'arrived' at the wrong time would get him in trouble.
And that's the stuff that shows up in Kenji's data as weird ETAs, by the way. Drivers who never tap arrived.
Yes. I filter those out. There are a lot.

So the new flow fixes each one. Phone-number login with an SMS code, no passwords at all. A three-step permissions primer — a screen before each system dialog that says, in plain words, what we use location for and that we stop tracking when your shift ends. And a practice route. A fake five-stop route on a map of their own depot, where they can tap through arrived, delivered, photo, signature, without anything real happening. We prototyped it and tested it with eleven drivers. Ten got through to the end without help. The eleventh had a cracked screen, which, I'm counting that as a hardware issue.
That's a pass. I'm calling that a pass.
And the target is below fifteen?

Below fifteen percent drop-off before first route. I think we can get closer to ten, but fifteen is what I'd commit to. And for the business, the fleet sees it as faster ramp. A new driver productive on day one instead of day four.

That's real for Brightside, by the way. If Sacramento happens, that's sixty new vans and probably seventy, eighty new drivers in the first month. If thirty-eight percent of them bounce off the app, the expansion's going to feel terrible and they'll blame us. So this ties into the renewal too, just less loudly than live ETA.
Okay. So what does it take?

Design's mostly done. Engineering, it's about two frontend engineers for six weeks. The driver app side is the bulk of it — new screens, the primer, the practice route, which is basically a little sandbox mode.

Plus backend for the phone login. It touches auth, which means it touches everything. SMS provider, rate limits, account recovery when someone changes their number. That's not huge but it's not nothing. Maybe a week of backend from someone who knows the auth service.
And please, rate-limit the SMS endpoint from day one. Every company that adds SMS login gets a bill from someone abusing it to send texts. I'm not doing that incident review.
Noted, Ravi.

So here's my problem with it, and it's not the design, the design's great. Two frontend engineers for six weeks is twelve engineer-weeks. We don't have twelve. We don't even have twelve if live ETA and reliability both go to zero. Our frontend people are on v3 GA — the route detail, the migration wizard, Priya's badge from earlier. That's why we opened the two senior frontend reqs in the first place.
Where are we on hiring?
Two reqs open. Sam Rivera did the final round on Wednesday and was, honestly, the strongest frontend candidate we've seen this year. Daniel did the system design round.
Really strong. Shipped a driver-facing React Native app at his last company, actually knows what offline-first means. He asked better questions about our sync model than some people who work here.
Hannah's putting the offer together Monday. But even if Sam says yes on the spot, there's a notice period. Best case he starts mid-November. Realistic case, the week after Thanksgiving.
And the second req?
Pipeline's thin. Two phone screens next week. I wouldn't plan on a second hire landing this quarter.
Do we have a referral bonus for that? I know at least two frontend people from my last company who'd take a call.
We do, and please. Send them to Hannah today. Not Monday. Today.
Today. Got it.
What about a contractor? We used that React Native shop for the photo capture work last year, and they were fine.

They were fine. Better than fine, actually. I asked them last week, they can give us one person starting November 2nd. Only one. And a contractor needs someone on our side reviewing their code, so it's not totally free.
I'd take one contractor plus Sam when he lands over waiting until January. If we start in January, we don't see the drop-off number move until March, and the OKR is this quarter.

I hear you. I just want to be honest that one contractor starting November 2nd, plus a new hire ramping in December, plus the December freeze — that's not six weeks of two engineers. It's maybe four weeks of one and a half.
Then we sequence it. Phone login and the primer first, because that's where most of the drop is. Practice route second. If the practice route slips to January, I can live with that.
Okay, I like that. Phone login and primer first. Let's hold the actual staffing call until we've heard Ravi, because it's all the same nine weeks. Ravi, you're up.

Okay. I'll keep it short. I'm asking for one engineer for three weeks, starting as soon as possible. Three things. One: retry budgets with jitter on the dispatch workers. On the 24th, every worker retried at once, immediately, forever, and that's what turned a ten-second Redis failover into a forty-seven-minute outage. With a retry budget, each worker gets a limited number of retries per window, with randomized backoff, so they don't all stampede at the same moment.
That one's pretty contained, right?

That one's maybe four days, including testing it properly. Two: a circuit breaker between dispatch and the ETA service. When the ETA service is struggling, the breaker trips, we stop hammering it, and we fall back to the last good ETA — clearly marked as stale — instead of timing out or serving garbage that looks fresh. That's the one that matters most for anything customer-facing, including whatever we decide about tracking links. And three: an automated status page. Right now a human has to notice, decide it's an incident, log into the status page tool, and write something. On the 24th that took twenty-six minutes. I want our alerts to post an 'investigating' notice automatically within five minutes, and a human edits it after.
Dumb question, maybe. How often does a Redis failover even happen? Is this a once-a-year thing?

Not dumb. A few times a year, on our current setup. The provider does maintenance, a node gets replaced, it fails over. Usually nobody notices, because usually it happens at three in the morning. The 24th was mid-afternoon on a weekday, peak dispatch, so every worker was busy at the same moment. That's what made it bad. So the honest answer is it'll happen again. The goal is that next time it's a blip instead of an outage.

Can I just say, the third one — that's the one customers actually saw. Nobody at Brightside knows what a retry storm is. They know our status page said everything was fine while their customers were calling them. If I can tell Jordan 'it now updates automatically within five minutes,' that's worth more in the renewal conversation than almost anything else we could build.
Yeah. That's honestly why it's on the list. It's the cheapest of the three and it's the one people remember.

For what it's worth, I think this is non-negotiable. Not 'nice to have.' GA is going to put more traffic on the ETA service, not less — twenty-five percent of fleets on the 17th, everyone by December 1st. If we roll out to a hundred percent with the same retry behavior that caused the 24th, we're basically scheduling the next outage. And if we're also putting ETAs in front of end customers in any form, then it's not even a question.
I agree. I'd rather argue about the other two than this one. I can pull one person from the integrations pod starting Monday. They know the dispatch workers better than anyone.
That'd be ideal. And I'll pair with them on the circuit breaker, because the fallback behavior is the tricky part. What counts as stale, how old is too old, what the dispatcher UI shows.
Who was on call on the 24th, by the way? I never asked how that week went for them.

One of the solver folks, and it was rough. Got paged at 14:13, spent the first fifteen minutes thinking it was a solver bug because the symptoms were all on the routing side. Which is part of Ravi's point — the alerts told us something was wrong, not what. I'd like the status page automation to fix the 'nobody's sure if this is an incident yet' window too.
It will. If the ETA error rate crosses the threshold, it's an incident, the page goes up, and then we can argue about severity afterwards.
If the dispatcher UI is going to show a stale state, can you loop me in? Just so it's not a red banner that makes people panic. It should say what's happening and what to do.
Deal. Yeah, I'd rather it not be a red banner either.

And one more customer thing. Brightside asked for a written incident summary, and what they got from us was, honestly, a pretty thin email. Ravi, if you could give me an external version of the retro — timeline, cause, what we changed — I'll walk Jordan and Aisha through it myself. Once the fixes are actually in, not before.
Yeah, I can do that. I'll strip out the internal stuff and the Slack screenshots. Give me until the fixes land so I can say 'shipped' instead of 'planned.'
Perfect. 'Shipped' is the word I want.

Can I use this with Harbor & Pine? I know it sounds weird to bring up an outage, but Elena is going to find our status page history anyway. If I can say 'we had an incident, here's exactly what we changed,' that's a maturity story. RouteWise has outages too, they just don't talk about them.
Yes, but after it's shipped, not before. And run the wording past Ravi. I don't want a slide that says 'can never happen again,' because it can.
Please never write 'can never happen again.' Write 'we've removed the failure mode that caused it and added automated detection.' That's true.
Got it. That's a better sentence anyway.
Also, quick tangent — I saw the status page vendor wants to raise our price next year. Is that —
Different conversation. Please. I have opinions and they will take twenty minutes.
Fine. Parking it. Separate thread. So, Ravi, three weeks, one engineer, from Monday. Done by — what, the 23rd?

The 23rd is realistic. Retry budgets first, the first week. Then the circuit breaker. The status page automation can happen in parallel, it's mostly config and a webhook. And I want to do a Redis failover drill in staging before GA ramps. Like a fire drill, on purpose, on a Tuesday afternoon, so we see what actually happens.
Put the drill on the calendar now, or it won't happen.
I'll send it today.

Okay. I'm going to call that one now, because nobody's arguing. Reliability work goes first. It starts Monday, one engineer from integrations, Ravi pairing, target October 23rd, and nothing else on today's list preempts it. Everyone okay with that?
Yes.
Yes. Very yes.
Yes. And that's three of the nine weeks, for the record. Six left.
Thank you, all. Honestly, I expected to have to fight harder for that.
You'd have had to fight harder if you'd asked for two engineers. One for three weeks, scoped like that, is the easiest yes on today's list.
Six left. Okay. Now the actual hard part.

Okay. So here's where I've landed, and then I want you all to poke holes in it. We have six engineer-weeks left after reliability. Full live ETA is five plus design, onboarding wants twelve. We can't do both. So my proposal is we build a smaller thing. Call it Live ETA v0. A shareable tracking link, per stop, that shows the ETA and a status timeline — scheduled, out for delivery, three stops away, arriving, delivered. No live map. No moving dot, no driver location at all. From what Tom and Sofia said earlier, the actual problem for both accounts is 'when is it coming,' not 'where is the truck.' I think that's about two and a half engineer-weeks, and I'd like it shipped by November 6th. The full live map comes in Q1, properly designed, with the privacy work Priya described. Onboarding starts November 2nd with the contractor, phone login and primer first. And reliability goes first, starting Monday, which we've already said. Okay. Go. Tell me why it's wrong.

I'll start with whether two and a half is real. I think it is, actually, and the reason is the map is where all the cost lives. Without it, we don't need a driver app release, we don't stream location, we don't pay for map tiles. The status timeline comes from stop events we already have — the driver taps 'departed' on the previous stop, we know they're one away. So it's a tokenized link, a small public page, and the send, by SMS or email from the fleet. Two and a half is believable if the design is done by mid-October. And it depends on Ravi's circuit breaker, because the stale case has to be handled from day one.

And on the math. Nine weeks. Three for reliability, two and a half for v0, that's five and a half. Which leaves three and a half, and that covers the auth backend week for phone login and someone on our side reviewing the contractor's code. So — it works. On paper. With exactly zero slack, which I hate. But it works.

My worry is it's not what Marcus asked for. I mean, I'll be honest, the RouteWise demo has the dot. The dot moving on the map is the thing people remember from that demo. If I go back with 'we have a link, but no map,' I'm worried it sounds like we're shipping half a feature because we couldn't do the whole thing.

Okay, but — did Marcus ask for the dot, or did he ask for fewer phone calls? Because you told us earlier that dispatch spends a third of their day on 'where's my truck' calls, and that's the thing Dana sees as headcount. A link that says 'arriving between two-ten and two-twenty-five, three stops away' kills that phone call just as dead as a dot does. And then we show him the Q1 map with a date we actually believe in.

Yeah. No, that's fair. The calls are the pain. The dot is the demo. And if I'm positioning it, it's not 'half a feature.' It's 'we ship the part that solves your problem in five weeks, and the full map in Q1 with your data in it.' RouteWise can't say the second part, because they don't do anything with telematics data. Okay. I can sell that. I can actually sell that.

And for Brightside, I told you, Jordan has literally never said the word 'map.' His complaint is customers not knowing when their groceries are coming, and wrong delivery windows. November 6th is before we start the renewal conversation and before he decides on Sacramento. If I can walk into that with a link that's live and working, that's a completely different meeting.

Design-wise, v0 is very doable. It's about a week. It's one page, mostly text, and it's mobile web, which is easy. And honestly, no map solves the driver privacy question for now, because there's no driver location to leak. I'd brand it with the fleet's logo and a small 'powered by Tandem.' I can have it ready for Daniel by the 16th.
Okay. I'm in. On one condition.
Go.

Tom resets expectations with Harbor & Pine in writing. Not on a call. An email to Marcus that says exactly what v0 is, what the date is, and that the map is Q1. Because if Dana's evaluation doc says 'live tracking this quarter' and we ship a link with no map, we've done the June thing again, just more slowly. And when it goes wrong, it's my team that gets asked why we didn't deliver what was promised.
In writing.
In writing. And cc Asher.

Okay. I'll be honest, I don't love it. It's an awkward email to send to a champion three weeks before a decision. There's a non-zero chance Marcus forwards it to Dana with a sad face, and then I'm explaining to Dana, who I've never met, why we changed our answer. But — fine. You're right. It's better that I reset it now than he finds out on November 6th. And if I frame it as 'here's what you get in five weeks, and here's the full version with a date,' that's actually a stronger position than a vague 'this quarter.'

For what it's worth, I don't think you did it carelessly. I think you were on the spot and you picked the answer that kept the deal alive. I'd just rather we fix it this week than in November, when it's way more expensive.
Thank you, Tom. Really.
I'll draft it this weekend, send it to you and Maya Monday, and it goes to Marcus Tuesday. The 6th.
I'll red-pen it. Gently.
You have never red-penned anything gently in your life.
First time for everything.

Can I say something? About v0. This is the first time my ETAs go directly to end customers. A dispatcher knows an ETA is an estimate. An end customer sees '2:14' and waits at the door at 2:14. For urban stops my error is about nine minutes, for docks it's about twelve. So a single point time will be wrong most of the time, for exactly the customers who are asking for this feature. I think we should show a range instead. Like, 'arriving 2:10 to 2:25.' I can calibrate the width per stop type, so suburban stops get a narrow range and docks get a wider one, and the real arrival lands inside the range most of the time. Around eighty percent, I'd target.
Huh. Yeah. That's — yeah.

That's really good. And it's honest. We stop pretending to a precision we don't have. And it's cheap on our side. The ETA endpoint already computes a distribution under the hood, we just throw everything away except the middle. So exposing a lower and upper bound is a small change. The calibration is the hard part, and that's Kenji's.
Honestly, that's better for sales, too. RouteWise shows a single time, and Marcus already told me their ETAs are off half the time. 'Our window is right four out of five times' — that's a pitch.
Please don't say four out of five until I've measured it.
I will not say four out of five until you have measured it. On the record.

Design-wise, a range is actually easier. And it can tighten as the van gets closer. 'Arriving 2:10 to 2:25' in the morning, then 'two-fifteen to two-twenty' when they're one stop away. People get that intuitively, it's like a pizza tracker.

Yes. The range should narrow when it's closer, that's natural, the uncertainty goes down. I need about two weeks to calibrate it properly. By October 23rd. And I want to use the Brightside shadow-mode data too, so the urban ranges are based on their actual stops.
And Jordan's complaint after the outage was literally wrong delivery windows. A window that's actually right is the fix for the thing he's mad about.
And when the circuit breaker trips, the link should widen the range or say 'updating,' not show a confident stale time.
Yes. Stale should mean wider, or no number at all.

Okay. Let me say the whole thing back, so it's in the recording and nobody can claim later they heard something else. One: reliability goes first. Starts Monday, one engineer from integrations with Ravi, done by October 23rd, nothing preempts it. Two: Live ETA v0. A tracking link with an ETA range and a status timeline, no live map, no driver location. About two and a half engineer-weeks, ships November 6th. Daniel owns the tech design, Priya owns the page design, Kenji owns the range calibration. Three: the full live map is Q1, and we scope it in December. Four: onboarding starts November 2nd with one contractor, phone login and primer first, the practice route can slip to January, Sam joins when he lands. Five: Tom resets expectations with Harbor & Pine in writing by Tuesday, the 6th. Sofia tells Brightside the v0 date by Friday, the 9th. And Maya, you'll turn all of this into a capacity plan by Monday. Does anyone disagree with any of that? Now's the time.
Not disagree. Just — zero slack. So if anything slips, it's v0 that slips, not reliability and not GA.
Agreed. That's the priority order. GA, reliability, v0, onboarding.
Hm. I'd want v0 above — no. No, fine. That's the order.
One thing I'd call open, not decided. How the link gets sent. SMS or email, and whether we pay for the SMS or the fleet does. That changes the cost a lot at Harbor & Pine's volume.
Open. Put it in the tech design with a recommendation, and we'll decide it async.

Okay, last section, and then you all get your Friday back. OKRs. I'll read them, owners say yes or push back. Objective one: ship Routing v3 GA on November 17th. Owner Daniel, Maya accountable for staffing. Key results: twenty-five percent of eligible fleets on the 17th, all eligible fleets by December 1st, the ETA error dashboard split by mode is live before rollout, and we decide the urban-dense default by end of January.
Yes. I'd add 'API parity with v2' as a key result, because it's the thing that'll actually bite us, and I want it to be visible.
And to be clear on staffing, the six on GA stay on GA through December 1st. Nothing we decided today touches them. v0 comes out of the unallocated weeks, and so does onboarding.
Added, API parity goes in. Objective two: cut driver onboarding drop-off below fifteen percent. Owner Priya.

Yes, but I'd frame the key result as below fifteen percent on the pilot cohorts. With phone login and the primer live for three pilot fleets by December 11th, before the freeze. Full rollout and the practice route are Q1. I don't want to commit to the whole fleet base on one contractor and a new hire.

I'd sign up for that version. The other version I'd be lying. And I'll be the one reviewing the contractor's code for the first two weeks, until Sam's in. So if my reviews are slow in November, that's why.

Okay, pilot cohorts it is. Objective three: close Harbor & Pine by October 30th. Owner Tom. Key results: scope reset email to Marcus by October 6th, and a v0 preview in front of Marcus before the decision.

Yes. And can I show Marcus Priya's mockups before the 30th? Since v0 itself won't ship until the 6th. If he sees the actual page with the range on it, I think it lands way better than me describing it.
Design will be ready on the 16th. You can show mockups after that. Just — mockups. Not a promise about pixels.
Not a promise about anything. I've learned my lesson. For this quarter, anyway.
I'll take it.

Objective four: keep Brightside. Renewal on January 31st, and set up the Sacramento expansion. Owner Sofia. Key results: tell Brightside the v0 date by October 9th, v0 live for Brightside on November 6th, urban-dense shadow mode for them, and the external incident summary once Ravi's fixes ship.

Yes. And I'd like to add a check-in with Jordan and Aisha in mid-November, after v0's been live a week, so I'm not walking into the renewal blind. I'll set that up. And honestly, if v0 is live and the status page fix is in, I think I can turn the Sacramento conversation from 'are you going to keep us' into 'how fast can you onboard sixty vans.' Which, conveniently, is Priya's objective too.
Good. And Ravi, reliability isn't an objective on its own, but I want it on the doc as a health metric so we keep looking at it.
Status page posts within five minutes of an incident starting, no retry storms on a failover, and the drill done in staging before GA ramps. That's it. If those three hold, I'm happy.

Perfect. So, dates, in order. Monday the 5th: reliability work starts, and Maya's capacity plan. Tuesday the 6th: Tom's email to Marcus. Wednesday the 7th: I send the final OKR doc. Friday the 9th: Daniel's v0 tech design, and Sofia tells Brightside. The 16th: Priya's v0 page design. The 23rd: reliability done, Kenji's range calibration done. November 2nd: onboarding starts. November 6th: v0 ships. November 10th: code freeze. November 17th: GA. Did I miss anything?
The 9th works for the tech design. Priya, I'll need even a rough wireframe by Wednesday, so I know what the page actually has to fetch.
You'll have a sketch Wednesday.
Sam's offer goes out Monday. Not on your list, but it's on mine.
Right. Hannah's sending that Monday. Okay. Anything else? Kenji, you've been quiet, and the one thing you said changed the plan, so — anything else?
No. I'm good. I'll start on the calibration Monday.
Can we add 'we actually decided things' as an OKR? Because I'd like credit for that one.

You can have it as a key result for the meeting. One out of one. And one more thing for the doc, while I have everyone. Tom and I are going to sit down next week on how commitments get made on sales calls, so the June thing and the Tuesday thing don't happen a third time. Not a punishment. A process. Something like, if it's not on the roadmap, you say 'let me check with product,' and I get back to the customer within two business days.
Two days I can work with. Honestly, I'd love a script for it. 'Let me check with product' sounds weak unless the answer comes back fast.
It'll come back fast. That's my side of the deal.
Can I get that same two-day rule for customer asks? Because Brightside asked twice and the honest answer both times was 'we'll see.'
Yes. Same rule. Write it into the doc.
Honestly, this was the least painful planning meeting we've had all year.
It was painful for about twelve minutes in the middle.
That was mostly me. Sorry, Maya. Genuinely. I'll send the draft email to you both Sunday night, probably. Please don't reply Sunday night.
It's fine. You owned it. That's all I wanted.
And my headset held up the whole hour. That's the real win.
Okay. Thanks, everyone. Seriously. This was hard and it was good. Recording and notes will be in the folder. Have a good weekend.
Bye, everyone.
Have a good weekend.

general.tldr: Q4 is locked: Routing v3 GA on Nov 17, reliability fixes first (from Oct 5), a map-less Live ETA v0 that shows ETA ranges by Nov 6 with the full live map in Q1, and the onboarding redesign starting Nov 2 with one contractor. Tom will reset his "this quarter" live ETA promise to Harbor & Pine in writing by Oct 6.

items.text: Choose Q4 priorities the team actually believes in, with about 11 engineers of capacity before on-call and holidays.

After GA, committed integrations work, on-call, Thanksgiving and the Dec 14 freeze, only about 9 engineer-weeks are unallocated. Live ETA (5), reliability (3) and onboarding (12) all compete for them.
Routing v3 beta beat its target. Across 6 fleets: 11% fewer miles (about 8–8.5% less drive time, not "11% faster") and on-time delivery up from 91.2% to 94.6%, against a 93% goal.
Tom told Harbor & Pine on Tuesday that live ETA sharing would be "ready this quarter". It is probably now in Marcus's evaluation doc for CFO Dana Whitfield.

Live ETA v0 replaces the full feature for Q4. It is a tracking link with an ETA range and a status timeline, with no map and no driver location. About 2.5 engineer-weeks, shipping Nov 6. The full live map moves to Q1.
Kenji's idea was adopted: show an ETA range ("arriving 2:10–2:25") rather than a point time. ETA error is about 9 min on dense urban stops and about 12 min at loading docks.
Reliability work goes first and nothing preempts it: one engineer for 3 weeks from Mon Oct 5, targeting Oct 23.
If anything slips, the priority order is GA, then reliability, then v0, then onboarding.
Q3 shipped the solver migration, beta rollout tooling and dispatch board filters. The CSV import rewrite slipped about 3 weeks after 2 engineers moved to beta support.
The ML ETA model's MAE improved from 6.1 to 4.3 minutes on beta fleets.
Sep 24 outage: 47 minutes (14:12–14:59 UTC). A Redis failover set off a retry storm from the dispatch workers. 312 fleets were affected, and the status page was only updated after 26 minutes.
Brightside's Jordan called Sofia directly about stale ETAs and the "all systems operational" status page. It was also his second request for live ETA sharing. Renewal is Jan 31 at $145k ARR.
Harbor & Pine: 420 trucks, about $310k ARR, decision Oct 30, against the cheaper RouteWise. Marcus Hill is the champion. CFO Dana Whitfield signs and has never been on a call.
Three more late-stage deals (two Texas grocery chains and a Denver parcel fleet) total roughly Harbor & Pine's ARR, and all want v3.

In GA on Nov 17: the new solver as default for new fleets, a migration wizard for existing fleets (all moved by end of January), Kenji's ETA model, time windows and break rules, and v2 API parity. Multi-day routes and EV charging move to Q1.
Code freeze is Nov 10. Rollout: 25% of eligible fleets on Nov 17, 50% the week after, all by Dec 1.
Six engineers stay on GA through Dec 1. Maya will not move anyone off it.

Urban-dense ETA mode cuts urban error from about 8.9 to about 6 min, but has only been tested on 2 fleets. It ships behind a per-fleet flag, off by default, with Brightside first after a week of shadow mode.
The full version is about 5 engineer-weeks: location streaming, a tokenized public link, a live map and map tile costs. It is in no one's plan.
Brightside has asked twice. Jordan ties it to the Jan 31 renewal and to a March Sacramento launch (+60 vans).
It is a design project too. This is the first end-customer surface, it raises driver privacy questions and needs a stale-ETA state, and the full map needs at least 2 weeks of design.
Harbor & Pine's real pain is phone calls: dispatch spends about a third of the day on "where's my truck" calls, which Dana sees as headcount.
38% of new drivers never finish their first route. They drop at three points: email and password login, permissions asked with no context, and a scary live first route.
New flow: phone-number login, a 3-step permissions primer and a practice route. In the prototype, 10 of 11 drivers finished unaided. Target is below 15% drop-off.

It needs about 2 frontend engineers for 6 weeks plus about 1 week of auth backend. Sam Rivera's offer goes out Monday, with a mid-November start at best. A React Native contractor is available from Nov 2.
Three fixes: retry budgets with jitter on dispatch workers, a circuit breaker that falls back to a clearly stale ETA, and an automated status page that posts within 5 minutes.
Daniel called it non-negotiable, because GA increases load on the ETA service and v0 puts ETAs in front of end customers.
A Redis failover drill will run in staging before the GA ramp.
Ship Routing v3 GA on Nov 17 (owner Daniel, Maya accountable). API parity was added as a KR.
Get onboarding drop-off below 15% on pilot cohorts, with phone login and the primer live for 3 pilot fleets by Dec 11 (owner Priya).
Close Harbor & Pine by Oct 30 (owner Tom), including the scope-reset email and a v0 preview with mockups.
Keep Brightside: renewal Jan 31, set up the Sacramento expansion, and a mid-November check-in (owner Sofia).
Reliability health metric: the status page posts within 5 minutes, no retry storms on failover, and the drill is done before the GA ramp.
Mon Oct 5: reliability work starts, Maya's capacity plan is due, and Sam Rivera's offer goes out.
Tue Oct 6: Tom emails Marcus to reset live ETA scope, cc Asher and Maya.
Wed Oct 7: Asher sends the final OKR doc, including the two-business-day rule for off-roadmap asks.
Fri Oct 9: Daniel's v0 tech design is due and Sofia tells Brightside the v0 date. Oct 16: Priya's page design. Oct 23: reliability and Kenji's range calibration are done.
Nov 2 onboarding starts, Nov 6 v0 ships, Nov 10 code freeze, Nov 17 GA.

decisions.tldr: Asher made the call on a scoped-down Live ETA v0 (no map, with ETA ranges, Nov 6) so reliability, GA and onboarding all fit in about 9 free engineer-weeks. Maya's condition was that Tom resets the Harbor & Pine promise in writing.

items.text: Urban-dense ETA mode ships in GA behind a per-fleet flag, off by default. Decided by Asher with Daniel and Maya, because it has only been validated on 2 fleets and a bad default would be a GA regression.
The urban-dense flag gets an end date: by end of January it is either made the default or deleted. Maya set this after Daniel raised the risk of permanent flags.
Brightside gets a week of shadow mode before urban-dense is enabled for them. Kenji's condition, because it is untested on their stop mix.
Nobody is pulled off GA to build live ETA. Maya refused, Daniel backed her, and Tom accepted: GA is the board-level date, and the migration wizard is a known risk.

Reliability work goes first: one integrations engineer plus Ravi, from Mon Oct 5, target Oct 23, and nothing preempts it. Asher called it with unanimous agreement, since GA increases load and v0 exposes ETAs publicly.

Live ETA v0 replaces the full feature for Q4. It is a per-stop tracking link with an ETA and a status timeline, with no live map and no driver location, about 2.5 engineer-weeks, shipping Nov 6. Asher proposed it because the customers' real problem is "when", not "where". Daniel confirmed the estimate and Maya confirmed it fits capacity.
The full live map is deferred to Q1 and will be scoped in December, with Priya's privacy design.

v0 shows an ETA range ("arriving 2:10–2:25"), not a point time. The range narrows as the van gets closer and widens or says "updating" when data is stale. Kenji proposed it because point ETAs would be wrong most of the time for urban and dock stops. Daniel, Tom and Priya endorsed it.
Tom resets Harbor & Pine's expectations in writing by Oct 6. This was Maya's condition for agreeing to v0, to avoid repeating the June over-commitment. Tom agreed, reluctantly.
Onboarding starts Nov 2 with one contractor, phone login and primer first. The practice route may slip to January, and Sam Rivera joins when he lands. This follows Priya's sequencing proposal.
Priority order if anything slips is GA, then reliability, then v0, then onboarding. Asher decided it after Maya flagged zero slack. Tom briefly wanted v0 higher, then agreed.
The onboarding OKR is measured on pilot cohorts (3 fleets by Dec 11), not the whole fleet base. Priya proposed it and Maya agreed, given one contractor plus a new hire.
New process: any off-roadmap customer or prospect ask gets "let me check with product" and an answer within two business days. Asher and Tom agreed, and Sofia extended it to customer asks.
How v0 links get sent (SMS or email) and who pays for SMS, which matters at Harbor & Pine's volume. Daniel will put a recommendation in the tech design, and the decision will be made async.
There is no fix this quarter for loading-dock ETA error (about 12 min, long tail). It needs dock-wait data, possibly from Harbor & Pine's Samsara feed.
Will Marcus, and Dana behind him, accept v0 plus a Q1 map instead of the promised "this quarter" live ETA?
Will Sam Rivera accept, and when does he start? Best case is mid-November, realistically after Thanksgiving. The second frontend req is unlikely to land this quarter.
The status page vendor's price increase was parked for a separate thread.

ask.q: What did we decide about live ETA?
ask.a: We're not building the full live map this quarter. Instead, Live ETA v0 ships Nov 6. It is a per-stop tracking link that shows an ETA range and a status timeline (scheduled, out for delivery, three stops away, arriving, delivered), with no map and no driver location, for about 2.5 engineer-weeks. The full live map moves to Q1 and will be scoped in December. If anything slips, v0 slips before GA or reliability.

Tom resets Harbor & Pine in writing by Oct 6. Maya owns the capacity plan (Oct 5). Daniel owns the v0 tech design (Oct 9) and the GA OKR. Priya owns the v0 page design (Oct 16) and the onboarding OKR. Ravi owns the reliability fixes (Oct 23). Sofia tells Brightside the v0 date by Oct 9. Kenji calibrates ETA ranges by Oct 23. Asher sends the final OKR doc on Oct 7.

ask.q: What's the risk with the ETA model?
ask.a: The 4.3-minute MAE is an average. Error is about 8.9 minutes on dense urban stops and about 12 minutes at loading docks, with some stops off by 30, because dock wait time isn't observed. Urban-dense mode brings urban error to about 6 minutes but has only been tested on 2 fleets, so it ships behind a flag. Because v0 shows ETAs to end customers, the team will display a calibrated range instead of a point time.

ask.q: What did Tom promise Harbor & Pine?
ask.a: On a Tuesday call, Tom told Marcus Hill that live ETA sharing would be "ready this quarter". He gave no date or scope, but Marcus wrote it down and it is likely in the evaluation doc for CFO Dana Whitfield. Tom owned it in the meeting. He agreed to email Marcus by Oct 6 resetting the scope to v0 on Nov 6, with the full map in Q1.

Kenji warned that the ETA model is much weaker on dense urban stops (about 8.9 min) and loading docks (about 12 min), and wanted a week of shadow mode before enabling urban-dense mode for Brightside. His key point was that v0 puts ETAs in front of end customers, who treat a point time literally, so v0 should show a range like "arriving 2:10–2:25". He'll calibrate it per stop type by Oct 23, targeting about 80% coverage.

ask.q: What's the plan for driver onboarding?
ask.a: 38% of new drivers drop off before their first route. Priya's redesign adds phone-number login, a 3-step permissions primer and a practice route, aiming for below 15%. Work starts Nov 2 with one contractor, with phone login and the primer first. Sam Rivera joins if he accepts, and the practice route may slip to January. The OKR is measured on 3 pilot fleets live by Dec 11.
